<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and with real rhetorical force, but CON built a tighter, more sustained line of attack. From the opening, CON reframed the debate around irreversibility of self-propagating drives, then in Rebuttal 1 caught PRO retreating to "self-limiting" and "marked, fading" constructs to answer ecological risk fears — pointing out this defends exactly the reversible alternative CON proposed, not the resolution's actual irreversible subject. PRO never fully escaped this trap: in Rebuttal 2 and even the closing, PRO's own "risk ladder" (start with lower-persistence constructs, escalate "only if data warrant") mirrored CON's proposed sequencing almost exactly, letting CON repeatedly declare "that is my position, not a rebuttal to it." PRO's late circularity argument in closing (you can't validate a brake without outdoor release) was clever, but CON's closing response — that self-limiting outdoor trials can validate the brake without ever releasing a genuinely self-propagating drive — held up and closed the loophole. PRO's mortality-urgency framing and regulatory-capacity comparisons (vaccines, GM crops) were strong and never fully neutralized, keeping this competitive, but CON's consistent exploitation of PRO's own hedge gave CON the cleaner, more decisive path through the debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]-[B2.2] catching PRO's retreat to "self-limiting" constructs as an implicit concession of the resolution's actual (self-propagating) subject, reinforced in [B4.2] and [B5.3], was the decisive recurring exchange PRO never fully dislodged.</best_rebuttal>
